title: Why worry
hookLine: refreshing a tracking page at 3 a.m.; Shantideva sorts every worry into two piles
carry: patience: no second hurt on top of the first
tomorrow: someone hits you with a stick. who are you angry at?

cards: Three in the morning, and the phone lights up the ceiling. You're refreshing a tracking page for a package that won't move till dawn. Or rereading a message for the tenth time.
Or checking the forecast for a day still a week away. None of it changes anything. You know that.
You keep refreshing anyway. Shantideva has a two-line answer to yesterday's question, and it's so plain it almost sounds like a joke. It isn't.

teach.b: Here's the verse, close to his words. If something can be fixed, why be unhappy about it?
And if it can't be fixed, what good does being unhappy do? That's it. Two piles.
Pile one: things you can do something about. There, worry isn't needed, because action is. Pile two: things you can't change.
There, worry can't help, because nothing it does reaches the problem. Either way, the churning adds a second hurt on top of the first. This isn't Shantideva saying don't care.
It's the opposite. He sits this verse inside his chapter on patience, the strength to bear what's hard without being eaten by it.
Caring goes into pile one, as action. Pile two gets acceptance, and often, something kind for yourself instead. And a lot of worries turn out to be mixed.
The package can't be hurried, but the message can be answered in the morning. Sort it, and the night gets quieter.
Why worry: a question, not a scolding.

how: Buddhist teachers often quote Shantideva's 'if it can be remedied, why worry' verse when teaching patience with difficulty, pairing it with practical action on what can change.

o: a prayer recited to make bad news turn out better
a cheerful saying that nothing is ever really wrong
act on what you can fix, and let worry go on the rest

games.q: the sorting machine — tap the pairs.
p: pile one: it can be fixed
pile two: it can't be fixed
a second hurt on top of the first
split it, and act on the part you can

s: Shantideva's 'why worry' means don't care about your problems
caring goes into action on what can be fixed; worry is what he drops.
the verse sits in his chapter on patience
patience: bearing what's hard without being eaten by it.
the verse only helps with problems you can't fix
it covers both piles: act on what you can, and stop churning over what you can't.

games.q: your flight is canceled, and the next one leaves tomorrow. you'll miss a friend's party tonight. which move follows the verse?
o: call the friend and rebook now; then let the canceled flight go.
stay at the gate refreshing the app in case the flight comes back.
decide none of it matters, and skip telling the friend anything.
games.why: a mixed worry: the flight is pile two, the friend and the rebooking are pile one. act on one, release the other.

practice: Write one worry at the top of a page. Under it, answer one question: can I do anything about this? If yes, write the very next step, small enough for tomorrow.
If no, write one plain sentence, like not mine to fix tonight, and rest your eyes on it for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Why worry: Shantideva's two-pile verse. If it can be fixed, act; if it can't, worry won't help.

carryVoice: Here's your line for tonight: patience, no second hurt on top of the first. If it can be fixed, act; if it can't, why worry? Sleep well.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 6.10 (if there is a remedy, why be unhappy? if there is none, what use is being unhappy?)
